key_facts: **Infantile haemangioma** is the commonest tumour of infancy (about 4–10% of infants): absent or faint at birth, then rapid growth.
Most growth happens in the **first 1–3 months**; involution over years, often leaving fibrofatty tissue or telangiectasia.
High-risk sites: **periocular, airway/beard, lip, nasal tip, large segmental facial, perineal**, ulcerated, or 5 or more lesions.
Refer high-risk lesions early, ideally by about **4 weeks** of age; **propranolol** is first-line and specialist-initiated.
Five or more skin haemangiomas: liver ultrasound. Large facial segmental lesions: think PHACE.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: An **infantile haemangioma (IH)** is a benign vascular **tumour** of infancy. It is absent or a faint mark at birth, **grows rapidly** (mostly in the first 1–3 months, largely complete by about 5 months), plateaus, then **involutes** over years. About **4–10%** of infants are affected.

sub: More in girls, premature and low-birth-weight babies, and twins.

ul: Clonal endothelial proliferation, **GLUT-1 positive** (unlike malformations and congenital haemangiomas).
Risk factors: prematurity, low birth weight, female sex, multiple pregnancy, placental anomalies.
**"Wait and it will go away"**: most do, but high-risk ones need treatment in the early growth window.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: A haemangioma is a **benign proliferation of immature endothelial cells** that later switches off.

mech.t: Tissue hypoxia (possibly placental) induces HIF-1α and VEGF in a progenitor cell population.
GLUT-1–positive endothelial cells proliferate rapidly in the first months.
Endothelial cells undergo apoptosis and are replaced by fibrofatty tissue over years.
mech.caption: Natural history: appearance, rapid growth, slow involution.

mech.t: Beta-blockade causes vasoconstriction, reduces VEGF signalling and speeds involution.

histo: Lobules of capillaries lined by GLUT-1–positive endothelium (GLUT-1 negative in congenital haemangiomas and malformations).

sections.title: Clinical features

head: Type
Appearance
rows: Bluish, rubbery swelling under the skin

blocks: Haemangiomas can occur anywhere, most often on the head and neck. **5 or more** skin haemangiomas raise concern for **liver haemangiomas**. White surface change can herald **ulceration**.

fig.caption: Natural history of infantile haemangioma: appearance (0–2 weeks), rapid growth (1–6 months), slow involution, and completion (5–7+ years).

sub: Posterior fossa anomalies, Haemangioma (large facial segmental), Arterial, Cardiac (coarctation) and Eye anomalies: needs MRI/MRA, echo and eye review.
Lumbosacral segmental haemangioma with spinal and urogenital anomalies: spinal imaging.

ul: Usually **clinical**.
Ultrasound if deep, or uncertain against a malformation or soft-tissue mass. MRI for complex facial or segmental lesions.
Abdominal ultrasound if there are 5 or more skin lesions.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: Present at birth, flat, **grows with the child**, no rapid tumour growth
Fully formed at birth; different natural history
Later onset; often a pedunculated bleeding papule

sections.title: Management
blocks: Active observation with **photo documentation**. Reassure parents about involution.

ul: Oral **propranolol** is first line for problematic IH. It is started and supervised by a specialist, with heart rate, BP and glucose monitoring. Feed regularly, and **hold doses if the baby is unwell or not feeding**.
Topical **timolol** for selected small, thin, superficial lesions (off-label; NICE ESUOM47).
Wound care, analgesia and antibiotics for ulceration; laser or surgery for selected residual changes.

ladder.t: Oral propranolol, specialist-initiated with monitoring; hold doses if not feeding or unwell.

refer.t: Periocular, airway/beard, lip, nasal tip, segmental facial, perineal, ulcerated or ≥5 lesions: refer ideally by about 4 weeks of age.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: High-risk haemangioma sites (listed above): **do not wait to see if it goes away**.
Stridor or noisy breathing with a beard-area haemangioma: **urgent**.
Ulcerated or bleeding haemangioma.

blocks.h4: Refer promptly (ideally by about 4 weeks of age if high risk)

ul: **Periocular** (risk to vision and amblyopia)
**Beard or airway** distribution (risk of stridor)
**Lip or perioral** (feeding)
Nasal tip, large facial, or **segmental** (PHACE risk with large facial segmental lesions)
**Perineal or flexural** (ulceration)
**Ulcerated, bleeding or rapidly enlarging**
**5 or more** skin lesions
Breast (girls) or large scalp lesions
Ulceration (painful, scarring), bleeding, amblyopia, airway obstruction, feeding problems, disfigurement; heart failure with large liver haemangiomas.
Most involute; residual skin changes are common in large or deep lesions.

pearls: The rapid growth window is early, so **late referral misses the easiest window for treatment**.
IP role: recognise high-risk sites, explain that beta-blockers are specialist-supervised, and support dressings for ulceration under the specialist plan.
BAD patient leaflet and the Birthmark Support Group are useful for families.

quiz.q: When does most haemangioma growth occur?
quiz.a: In the first 1–3 months; largely complete by about 5 months.

quiz.q: Which marker distinguishes IH from malformations?

quiz.a: Oral propranolol, started by a specialist.
